The independent republics of Central Asia are the five states that came out of the break-up of the Soviet Union in 1991: Kazakhstan, Uzbekistan, Turkmenistan, Kyrgyzstan and Tajikistan. Together they have about 76 million people.

They did not seek independence; it came to them when the Soviet Union dissolved. Their borders were the ones the Soviets had drawn in the 1920s, and their first leaders were mostly the old Communist party chiefs.

Their paths since:

  • Kazakhstan: ruled by Nursultan Nazarbayev until 2019; grew rich on oil and moved its capital to Astana. Protests in January 2022 were put down with help from Russian-led troops.
  • Uzbekistan: ruled harshly by Islam Karimov until his death in 2016; his successor opened the economy and ended forced labour in the cotton harvest.
  • Turkmenistan: one of the most closed states in the world, living on natural gas.
  • Kyrgyzstan: the most open politics, with presidents overthrown in 2005 in the Tulip Revolution and again in 2010.
  • Tajikistan: a civil war from 1992 to 1997, then long rule by one president.

The region sits between Russia, China, Iran and Afghanistan. Russia remains the main security partner and a major destination for migrant workers. China has become the biggest trade partner and investor, above all since the Belt and Road Initiative was announced in Kazakhstan in 2013.

The old Silk Road cities, Samarkand, Bukhara and Khiva, are now in Uzbekistan.
sum: The independent republics of Central Asia are the five states that came out of the break-up of the Soviet Union in 1991: Kazakhstan, Uzbekistan, Turkmenistan, Kyrgyzstan and Tajikistan. Together they have about 76 million people.
